section.title: Classical Stokes' theorem as generalized Stokes
section.p: kept everything flat. A plane region R had a boundary curve \partial R, and Green's theorem became \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. Now the region is allowed to bend into space. The boundary is still a curve, but the inside is a surface.

subsection.title: A tilted sheet and a boundary integral
subsection.p: Start with a tilted rectangular sheet in space: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,u+2v), \qquad 0\le u\le2,\quad 0\le v\le1. The parameter rectangle is D=[0,2]\times[0,1]. The surface orientation is determined by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. Since \mathbf r_u=(1,0,1), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(0,1,2), we get \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(-1,-2,1).
Now take the 1-form \omega=z\,dy. This form is built to be integrated along the boundary curve of the tilted sheet.

Instead of parametrizing the four boundary curves directly in space, pull the form back to the parameter rectangle. On the surface, x=u,\qquad y=v,\qquad z=u+2v. So dy=dv, and \mathbf r^*\omega=(u+2v)\,dv.
The boundary of D is positively oriented counterclockwise. Compute the integral around its four sides.
On the bottom side v=0, dv=0, so the contribution is 0.
On the right side u=2, v goes from 0 to 1, so \int_{\text{right}}(u+2v)\,dv = \int_0^1(2+2v)\,dv = 3.
On the top side v=1, dv=0, so the contribution is 0.
On the left side u=0, v goes from 1 down to 0, so \int_{\text{left}}(u+2v)\,dv = \int_1^0 2v\,dv = -1.
Adding the four sides gives \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega = \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = 3-1 = 2. }

Now compute the surface side. Since \omega=z\,dy, we have d\omega=dz\wedge dy. Pull this back: dz=d(u+2v)=du+2\,dv, so
\mathbf r^*(d\omega) \amp= (du+2\,dv)\wedge dv\\ \amp= du\wedge dv.
Therefore
\int_S d\omega \amp= \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega)\\ \amp= \int_D du\wedge dv\\ \amp= \operatorname{Area}(D)\\ \amp= 2.
So \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }

subsection.p: The computation contains the whole theorem. The boundary integral on the surface was turned into a boundary integral on the parameter rectangle. Then Green's theorem took over.

subsection.title: Pullback to a parameter domain
subsection.p: A C^2 regular parametrization, one-to-one in the interior and tracing the patch's boundary once, \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)) lets us translate forms in space into forms in the parameter plane.

For a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, the pullback is \boxed{ \mathbf r^*\omega = P(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d x(u,v) + Q(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d y(u,v) + R(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d z(u,v). } Here dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv, dy=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv, and dz=z_u\,du+z_v\,dv.
The pullback does two jobs at once. It substitutes the parametrization into the coefficients, and it replaces dx,dy,dz by the coordinate changes caused by du and dv.
For boundary integrals, \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega, } provided the boundary orientation on S is induced from the boundary orientation on D.
The most important identity is \boxed{ d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega). } This is the chain rule in form language. It says that pulling back and differentiating fit together.

Here is the coordinate justification. Write \omega=\sum_i F_i\,dx_i and \mathbf r^*\omega=A\,du+B\,dv, where A=\sum_i F_i(\mathbf r)(x_i)_u and B=\sum_i F_i(\mathbf r)(x_i)_v. The product and chain rules give B_u-A_v=\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jF_i)(\mathbf r) \bigl((x_j)_u(x_i)_v-(x_j)_v(x_i)_u\bigr). Terms containing (x_i)_{uv}-(x_i)_{vu} cancel because \mathbf r is C^2. The displayed coefficient is exactly the coefficient obtained by pulling back d\omega=\sum_{i,j}\partial_jF_i\,dx_j\wedge dx_i. This proves the identity used here without assuming Stokes' theorem.

Now apply Green's theorem on D: \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega). Using d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega), we get \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega). Translated back to the surface, this becomes \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.
That is Stokes' theorem.

subsection.title: Curl as the exterior derivative of a 1-form
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a vector field, and let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be its work 1-form.

Compute d\omega:
d\omega \amp= dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy+dR\wedge dz\\ \amp= (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz\\ \amp\quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx\\ \amp\quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.
In words: \boxed{ \text{the exterior derivative of the work form is the flux form of the curl.} }
This is why the right side of classical Stokes' theorem contains curl.

exercise.title: Why does curl show up at all?

statement.p: The right-hand side of Stokes' theorem could have been any combination of derivatives of P,Q,R. Why is it exactly the curl that appears, rather than, say, the divergence or some other mixture? What feature of d\omega forces this particular answer?

hint.p: Look back at the coefficients that came out of computing d\omega for a work 1-form. Nobody chose them by hand — ask what produced them.

subsection.title: Boundary circulation equals surface curl
subsection.p: Now the theorem can be written in both languages.

theorem.title: Classical Stokes' theorem as generalized Stokes

statement.p: Let S be an oriented compact piecewise smooth surface in space, with piecewise smooth boundary \partial S. Give \partial S the boundary orientation compatible with the orientation of S.
Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be a C^1 1-form on an open set containing S. Then \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }

subsection.p: The forms statement is the generalized Stokes theorem with M=S, \qquad \omega\text{ a }1\text{-form}. The vector statement is the classical formula students often learn first.
The left side is boundary circulation. The right side is curl passing through the surface.

subsection.title: A curved surface with the same boundary
subsection.p: Let \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy.

Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2, \qquad z\ge0, oriented by the upward/outward normal. Its boundary is the circle C:\quad x^2+y^2=a^2,\qquad z=0, oriented counterclockwise as viewed from above.

Now compute the surface integral. Since d\omega=dx\wedge dy, the integral \int_S dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of the shadow of S on the xy-plane. With upward orientation, that shadow is the disk x^2+y^2\le a^2 with positive orientation. Therefore \boxed{ \int_S d\omega=\int_S dx\wedge dy=\pi a^2. } Again, \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }
The hemisphere and the flat disk have the same boundary. For this form, both surfaces give the same answer because Stokes' theorem only sees the boundary.

exercise.title: What does “only sees the boundary” mean?

statement.p: We bent the surface from a flat disk into a dome, yet the value of \int_S d\omega did not budge. What is the theorem really telling us about which features of a surface affect the answer and which are irrelevant? Could you replace the hemisphere with a wildly crumpled sheet and still get \pi a^2?

hint.p: Both sides of \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega share one curve. Think about what would have to change for the answer to change.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem is a sign-sensitive theorem. It is also sensitive to holes and singularities.

p.em: The boundary orientation must be compatible.

subsection.p: Use the disk x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0, with upward orientation, and use \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy, so \int_S d\omega=\pi.
The compatible boundary orientation is counterclockwise. With that orientation, \int_{\partial S}\omega=\pi.
If we walk the same boundary clockwise, the boundary integral becomes -\pi. The surface integral has not changed. The problem is not the theorem; the boundary orientation was wrong.

p.em: Every boundary component must be included.

subsection.p: Let A=\{(x,y,0):1\le x^2+y^2\le4\} be a flat annulus with upward orientation. Its boundary has two components: C_{\text{outer}}:\ x^2+y^2=4, and C_{\text{inner}}:\ x^2+y^2=1. The compatible orientation is counterclockwise on the outer circle and clockwise on the inner circle.
For \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy, we have d\omega=dx\wedge dy. Therefore \int_A d\omega=\operatorname{Area}(A)=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
On a counterclockwise circle of radius r, \int\omega=\pi r^2. So the outer boundary contributes 4\pi, while the clockwise inner boundary contributes -\pi. Thus \int_{\partial A}\omega=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
If we forgot the inner boundary, the left side would be 4\pi, not 3\pi. The hole has a rim, and Stokes' theorem counts that rim with its induced sign.

p.em: The form must be defined on the whole surface.

subsection.p: Consider \alpha= -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. This form is defined away from the z-axis. Where it is defined, d\alpha=0.

A careless use of Stokes' theorem on the flat unit disk would say \int_C\alpha=\int_D d\alpha=0. But the form is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies in the disk. Stokes' theorem cannot be used there.

If we remove a small disk around the origin, the theorem works again. The new surface is an annulus. Its outer boundary contributes 2\pi, and its inner boundary contributes -2\pi. The total boundary integral is 0, matching \int d\alpha=0 on the annulus.
The missing point was not harmless. It carried the circulation.

statement.p: The form \alpha satisfies d\alpha=0 everywhere it is defined, so its exterior derivative seems to contribute nothing. Yet the loop integral came out to 2\pi, not 0. How can a single excluded point at the origin be responsible for all of that circulation, when the surface integrand vanishes everywhere it exists?

hint.p: Stokes' theorem needs \alpha defined on the whole surface. Ask what the disk contains that the form refuses to live at.

subsection.p: Stokes' theorem compares a boundary curve with a surface. But some surfaces have no boundary curve at all. A sphere has no rim. A closed box surface has no edge. Still, flux can pass through them. To read that situation as Stokes' theorem, the object inside must be one dimension higher: a solid region, with a 2-form on its boundary.
